newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court reinstates indictment against Nippon Paper.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court reinstates indictment against Nippon Paper.

text.p: The U.S. Court of Appeals has overturned a lower court's dismissal of a 1995 indictment against a Japanese fax paper manufacturer that the U.S. government accused of violating the Sherman Act through price-fixing activities affecting United States commerce.

In acknowledging the precedent-setting decision -- since no prior Sherman Act cases involved criminal conduct undertaken wholly outside the United States -- the Appeals Court found that "Section One of Sherman Act applies to wholly foreign conduct which has an intended and substantial effect in the United States."

The case stems from the December 1995 federal indictment against Jujo Paper Co., Ltd. and its successor entity, Nippon Paper Industries Co Ltd, of Japan for conspiring with unnamed co-conspirators to increase the prices of thermal fax paper to be sold throughout North America.

Pursuant to agreements reached during a number of meetings in Japan, Nippon Paper and other Japanese paper manufacturers, who were privy to the scheme, purportedly accomplished their objectives by selling their paper to unaffiliated trading houses in Japan on condition that the paper would be shipped and sold to subsidiaries in the United States who in turn sold it to American consumers at swollen prices.

The indictment noted that, subsequent to the agreement among co-conspirators, Nippon monitored the paper sales and confirmed that the prices charged to end users were those earlier arranged. The indictment charged that Nippon's activities had a substantial adverse affect on U.S. commerce and unreasonably restrained trade in violation of the Sherman Act.

Nippon responded to the indictment by arguing that its actions, if they occurred at all, took place entirely in Japan and the application of the Sherman Act is unprecedented when "one nation seeks to apply its criminal laws to actions taken in a foreign country by nationals of that country." Federal court Judge Joseph Tauro agreed and dismissed the case.

However, the Appeals Court concluded that Nippon's conduct was illegal under both Japanese and American laws, and according to the U.S. indictment, Nippon orchestrated a conspiracy with the object of rigging prices in the United States. The Court reinstated the indictment and remanded the case for further proceedings.
